claim: SARS-CoV-2 transmission by aerosolized virus particles has been a major contributor to the spread of the virus.
source: Transmission by aerosolized virus particles has been a major contributor to the spread of SARS-CoV-2 (Zhang et al., 2020; Port et al., 2022; Boone and Gerba, 2007; Goldman, 2020; CDC, 2021a; Pitol and Julian, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Vaccines are highly efficient in preventing severe COVID-19 disease.
source: Although highly efficient in preventing severe disease, vaccines do not significantly reduce transmission of variants of concern (VOCs) (CDC, 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to CDC guidance.

claim: Vaccines do not significantly reduce transmission of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern.
source: Although highly efficient in preventing severe disease, vaccines do not significantly reduce transmission of variants of concern (VOCs) (CDC, 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to CDC guidance.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detectable mostly in fine aerosols in humans, as opposed to coarse aerosols.
source: As with influenza (Milton et al., 2013), SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detectable mostly in fine aerosols in humans, as opposed to coarse aerosols (Coleman et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on influenza and SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Superspreading events have been reported numerous times throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Superspreading events have been reported numerous times throughout the pandemic and are suggested to be a major driver (Sun et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Syrian hamster model recapitulates human contact, fomite and airborne short distance and fine aerosol transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: The Syrian hamster model has been widely used to study SARS-CoV-2 transmission Muñoz-Fontela et al., 2020; it recapitulates human contact, fomite and, importantly, airborne short distance and fine aerosol transmission (Port et al., 2022; Sia et al., 2020; Rosenke et al., 2020; Port et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: In the Syrian hamster model, highest efficiency of short-distance airborne transmission was observed before onset of weight loss and acute lung pathology.
source: In this model, highest efficiency of short-distance airborne transmission was observed before onset of weight loss and acute lung pathology, peaking at 1 day post inoculation and correlating to the highest virus loads in the upper respiratory tract of donor animals (Ganti et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Structural modeling and pseudotype-entry comparison suggested that the Syrian hamster model should recapitulate the entry-specific competitive advantage of Delta over Alpha observed in humans.
source: Structural modeling and pseudotype-entry comparison suggested that the Syrian hamster model should recapitulate the entry-specific competitive advantage of Delta over Alpha observed in humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and pseudotype-entry experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: No significant differences in weight loss were observed between Alpha and Delta variants in Syrian hamsters.
source: We observed no significant differences in weight loss or viral titers in lung or nasal turbinates between the variants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: No significant differences in viral titers in lung or nasal turbinates were observed between Alpha and Delta variants in Syrian hamsters.
source: We observed no significant differences in weight loss or viral titers in lung or nasal turbinates between the variants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: At 14 days post inoculation, hamsters mounted a robust anti-spike IgG antibody response.
source: At 14 DPI, hamsters (N=5) mounted a robust anti-spike IgG antibody response, and the overall binding pattern was similar between Alpha and Delta (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: The overall binding pattern of anti-spike IgG antibodies was similar between Alpha and Delta variants.
source: At 14 DPI, hamsters (N=5) mounted a robust anti-spike IgG antibody response, and the overall binding pattern was similar between Alpha and Delta (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Homologous virus was neutralized significantly better compared to the heterologous variant in a live virus neutralization assay.
source: In a live virus neutralization assay, homologous virus was neutralized significantly better as compared to the heterologous variant Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G), but no significant difference was determined between the neutralization capacity against the respective homologous variant (median reciprocal virus neutralization titer = 320 (Alpha anti-Alpha)/ 320 (Delta anti-Delta), p=0.9568, N=5, ordinary two-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a live virus neutralization assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: No significant difference was determined between the neutralization capacity against Alpha and Delta homologous variants.
source: In a live virus neutralization assay, homologous virus was neutralized significantly better as compared to the heterologous variant Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G), but no significant difference was determined between the neutralization capacity against the respective homologous variant (median reciprocal virus neutralization titer = 320 (Alpha anti-Alpha)/ 320 (Delta anti-Delta), p=0.9568, N=5, ordinary two-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of neutralization assay data.

claim: Oral swabs remained positive for gRNA and sgRNA until 7 days post inoculation.
source: Oral swabs remained positive for gRNA and sgRNA until 7 DPI, but infectious virus dropped to undetectable levels after 4 DPI in most individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Infectious virus in oral swabs dropped to undetectable levels after 4 days post inoculation in most individuals.
source: Oral swabs remained positive for gRNA and sgRNA until 7 DPI, but infectious virus dropped to undetectable levels after 4 DPI in most individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: gRNA and sgRNA were detectable in cage air as early as 1 day post inoculation in 50% of air samples.
source: gRNA and sgRNA were detectable as early as 1 DPI in 50% of air samples and remained high through 5 DPI, while infectious virus peaked at on 2 DPI and was detectable for a shorter window, from 1 to 4 DPI (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Infectious virus in cage air peaked at 2 days post inoculation.
source: gRNA and sgRNA were detectable as early as 1 DPI in 50% of air samples and remained high through 5 DPI, while infectious virus peaked at on 2 DPI and was detectable for a shorter window, from 1 to 4 DPI (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Infectious virus in cage air was detectable from 1 to 4 days post inoculation.
source: gRNA and sgRNA were detectable as early as 1 DPI in 50% of air samples and remained high through 5 DPI, while infectious virus peaked at on 2 DPI and was detectable for a shorter window, from 1 to 4 DPI (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Virus was detectable and peaked earlier in oral swabs (approximately 24 hr post inoculation) than virus sampled from the air (approximately 48 hr post inoculation).
source: Virus was detectable and peaked earlier in oral swabs (approximately 24 hr post inoculation) than virus sampled from the air (approximately 48 hr post inoculation), and quantity of detected virus declined slower in the swabs (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Quantity of detected virus declined slower in oral swabs compared to air samples.
source: Virus was detectable and peaked earlier in oral swabs (approximately 24 hr post inoculation) than virus sampled from the air (approximately 48 hr post inoculation), and quantity of detected virus declined slower in the swabs (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: gRNA and sgRNA declined slower than infectious virus both in the air and in swabs.
source: gRNA and sgRNA declined slower than infectious virus both in the air and in swabs.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: Oral swab data was an imperfect proxy for airborne shedding due to a lag between peak swab shedding and peak airborne shedding.
source: Oral swab data was an imperfect proxy for airborne shedding, even when we directly quantified infectious virus titers. This was due to a lag between peak swab shedding and peak airborne shedding.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: Inferred within-host exponential growth and decay rates were similar for Alpha and Delta variants.
source: Inferred within-host exponential growth and decay rates were similar for the two variants.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling of within-host virus kinetics.

claim: For both Alpha and Delta variants, males shed more virus than females, even after accounting for males' higher respiration rates.
source: For both variants, males shed more virus than females, even after accounting for males' higher respiration rates in measurements of shedding into the air.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical modeling and experimental data.

claim: A slightly higher ratio of infectious virus to sgRNA in air samples was found for Delta than for Alpha.
source: We found a slightly higher ratio of infectious virus to sgRNA in air samples for Delta than for Alpha (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: Substantial individual-level heterogeneity in airborne shedding was found, even after accounting for sex and variant.
source: We also found substantial individual-level heterogeneity in airborne shedding, even after accounting for sex and variant (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pathology in nasal turbinates and lungs did not differ significantly between Alpha and Delta infected animals.
source: Pathology in nasal turbinates and lungs did not differ significantly between animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pathological changes were consistent with those described previously for COVID-19 in Syrian hamsters after intranasal inoculation with other SARS-CoV-2 strains.
source: Pathological changes were consistent with those described previously for COVID-19 in Syrian hamsters after intranasal inoculation with other SARS-CoV-2 strains (Rosenke et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published literature.

claim: Beginning at 2 days post inoculation, a separation of infected and control animals was observed in principal component analysis of plethysmography measures.
source: Beginning at 2 DPI, we observed a separation of infected and control animals.
evidence: The claim is based on principal component analysis of whole body plethysmography data.

claim: All SARS-CoV-2 infected animals visibly decreased activity levels after 2 days post inoculation.
source: This coincided with the observation that all SARS-CoV-2 animals visibly decreased activity levels after 2 DPI, reducing exploratory activity and grooming with sporadic short convulsions which may represent coughing.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data during the experiment.

claim: Cumulative Penh AUC values for all infected groups were increased compared to the sex-matched control hamsters.
source: Cumulative Penh AUC values for all infected groups were increased compared to the sex-matched control hamsters (p=0.022, Kruskal-Wallis test, N=4 for Alpha and Delta, N=5 for controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of whole body plethysmography data.

claim: Across each variant group, particle diameter size <0.53 µm was the most abundant.
source: Across each variant group, particle diameter size <0.53 µm was the most abundant (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by aerodynamic particle sizing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No consistent, significant overall change in the number of overall particles across all sizes was observed between groups.
source: No consistent, significant overall change in the number of overall particles across all sizes was observed between groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At baseline (0 days post inoculation), females across all groups produced a higher proportion of droplets in the 1–10 µm diameter range compared to males.
source: At baseline (0 DPI), females across all groups produced a higher proportion of droplets in the 1–10 µm diameter range compared to males (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by aerodynamic particle sizing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 3 days post inoculation, the particle profiles shifted toward smaller aerodynamic diameters in the infected groups.
source: At 3 DPI, the particle profiles shifted toward smaller aerodynamic diameters in the infected groups.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of aerodynamic particle sizing data.

claim: Females had a steeper decline at an average rate of 2.2 per day after inoculation in the percent of 1–10 μm particles when compared to males, while holding variant group constant.
source: Females had a steeper decline at an average rate of 2.2 per day after inoculation in the percent of 1–10 μm particles (and a steeper incline for <0.53 μm) when compared to males, while holding variant group constant.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple linear regression analysis of particle sizing data.

claim: The Delta group had a steeper decline at an average rate of 5.6 per day in the percent of 1–10 μm particles when compared to controls, while holding sex constant.
source: When we compared variant group while holding sex constant, we found that the Delta group had a steeper decline at an average rate of 5.6 per day in the percent of 1–10 μm particles (and a steeper incline for <0.53 μm); a similar trend, but not as steep, was observed for the Alpha group.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple linear regression analysis of particle sizing data.

claim: sgRNA in oral swabs taken on 1 day post inoculation varied between donor animals.
source: sgRNA in oral swabs taken on 1 DPI varied between animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: On 2 days post exposure, N=13/34 sentinels were positive for sgRNA in oral swabs.
source: On 2 DPE, N=13/34 sentinels were positive for sgRNA in oral swabs, N=19/34 on 3 DPE and N=27/34 on 5 DPE.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: All animals had only one variant detectable on day 3 post exposure in the attack rate experiment.
source: All animals had only one variant detectable on day 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: In total, 12 sentinels were infected with Alpha and 7 with Delta by 3 days post exposure in the attack rate experiment.
source: In total, 12 sentinels were infected with Alpha and 7 with Delta by 3 DPE.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: One superspreading event was observed in iteration A, in which one donor animal transmitted Alpha to all sentinels.
source: Interestingly, we observed one superspreading event in iteration A, in which one donor animal transmitted Alpha to all sentinels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: For the iterations with simultaneous exposure, attack rates were similar and statistically indistinguishable: Alpha = 50 %, Delta = 42.8%.
source: For the iterations with simultaneous exposure, attack rates were similar and statistically indistinguishable: Alpha = 50 %, Delta = 42.8%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: In one simultaneous exposure (iteration F), three sentinels had both Delta and Alpha detectable at 5 days post exposure.
source: In one simultaneous exposure (iteration F), three sentinels had both Delta and Alpha detectable at 5 DPE.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: No difference in virus replication or disease severity was observed between the sentinels infected with Alpha or Delta in the attack rate experiment.
source: No difference in virus replication or disease severity was observed between the sentinels infected with Alpha or Delta (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All Sentinels 1 demonstrated active shedding at 2 and 5 days post exposure in the transmission chain experiment.
source: While all Sentinels 1 demonstrated active shedding at 2 and 5 DPE, in the Sentinels 2 group no viral RNA was detected in 2/8 animals and no infectious virus in 4/8 by 5 DPE.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: In the Sentinels 2 group, no viral RNA was detected in 2/8 animals and no infectious virus in 4/8 by 5 days post exposure.
source: While all Sentinels 1 demonstrated active shedding at 2 and 5 DPE, in the Sentinels 2 group no viral RNA was detected in 2/8 animals and no infectious virus in 4/8 by 5 DPE.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: In the Sentinels 3 group, sgRNA and infectious virus were only detected robustly in one animal on 5 days post exposure.
source: In the Sentinels 3 group, sgRNA and infectious virus were only detected robustly in one animal on 5 DPE.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: All infected sentinels exhibited higher shedding on day 5 compared to day 2 in the transmission chain experiment.
source: In contrast to donor animals, all infected sentinels exhibited higher shedding on day 5 compared to day 2 2 DPI / 5 DPI Donors: median gRNA = 7.8 / 6.9 copies/mL (Log10), median sgRNA = 7.2 / 6.4 copies/mL (Log10), median infectious virus titer = 2.3 / 0.5 TCID50/mL (Log10); Sentinels 1 (median gRNA = 7.2 / 7.4 copies/mL (Log10), median sgRNA = 6.4 / 6.9 copies/mL (Log10), median infectious virus titer = 2.9 / 2.6 TCID50/mL (Log10); Sentinels 2=median gRNA = 3.7 / 5.4 copies/mL (Log10), median sgRNA = 1.8 / 3.0 copies/mL (Log10), median infectious virus titer = 0.5 / 1.6 TCID50/mL (Log10)) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The infectious shedding profile shifts later and decreases in magnitude with successive generations of transmission.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests that the infectious shedding profile shifts later and decreases in magnitude with successive generations of transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data in the transmission chain experiment.

claim: Lower exposure doses could cause lower and slower infections in the recipients.
source: This could be explained by lower exposure doses causing lower and slower infections in the recipients.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for observed data.

claim: Neither Alpha nor Delta variant significantly outcompeted the other in the transmission chain experiment.
source: To determine the competitiveness of the variants, we analyzed the relative composition of the two viruses using next generation sequencing (Figure 5F and G). Neither variant significantly outcompeted the other.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: In Donors, no variant was more prevalent across animals or clearly outcompeted the other within one host (median = 56.5% Delta, range = 40.3–69%).
source: In Donors, no variant was more prevalent across animals or clearly outcompeted the other within one host (median = 56.5% Delta, range = 40.3–69%).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: After the first transmission event, Delta outcompeted Alpha at 2 days post exposure (median = 87.3% Delta, range = 19–92.7%).
source: After the first transmission event, Delta outcompeted Alpha at 2 DPE (median = 87.3% Delta, range = 19–92.7%), while after the second transmission event, half (N=2/4) the animals shed either >80% either Alpha or Delta.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: Every sentinel animal exhibited a mixed infection at 2 days post exposure in the transmission chain experiment.
source: Notably, and in strong contrast to the dual donor experiments described above, every sentinel animal exhibited a mixed infection at 2 DPE, often with proportions resembling those in the donor.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: In the Sentinels 1 group, Alpha overtook Delta in three animals by 5 days post exposure.
source: By 5 DPI/DPE, no clear difference was observed in Donors (median = 60% Delta, range = 34.3–67.7%), but in the Sentinels 1 group Alpha overtook Delta in three animals (median = 68.3% Delta, range = 17–92.3%), while the reverse was never seen.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the transmission chain experiment.

claim: Within one host, Alpha was marginally more successful at outcompeting Delta in the oropharyngeal cavity.
source: This suggests that within one host, Alpha was marginally more successful at outcompeting Delta in the oropharyngeal cavity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from sequencing data.

claim: In Donor lungs, the percentage of Alpha was marginally higher on 5 days post inoculation (median = 42.3% Delta, range = 23.3–75.7%).
source: In Donor lungs, the percentage of Alpha was marginally higher on 5 DPI (median = 42.3% Delta, range = 23.3–75.7%).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from lung tissue.

claim: Swabs taken at 2 days post inoculation/exposure significantly predict variant patterns in swabs on 5 days post inoculation/exposure (Spearman's r=0.623, p=0.00436).
source: Swabs taken at 2 DPI/DPE did significantly predict variant patterns in swabs on 5 DPI/DPE (Spearman's r=0.623, p=0.00436) and virus competition in the lower respiratory tract (Spearman's r=0.60, p=0.00848).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of sequencing data.

claim: Oral swab samples taken on day 5 strongly correlate with both upper (Spearman's r=0.816, p=0.00001) and lower respiratory tract tissue samples (Spearman's r=0.832, p=0.00002) taken on the same day.
source: Oral swab samples taken on day 5 strongly correlate with both upper (Spearman's r=0.816, p=0.00001) and lower respiratory tract tissue samples (Spearman's r=0.832, p=0.00002) taken on the same day (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: In immunologically naive humans, peak SARS-CoV-2 shedding occurs multiple days after exposure and in some cases multiple days before onset of symptoms.
source: In immunologically naive humans, peak SARS-CoV-2 shedding occurs multiple days after exposure and in some cases multiple days before onset of symptoms (Jones et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Past studies in hamsters have shown that SARS-CoV-2 transmissibility is limited to the first 3 days.
source: Past studies in hamsters have shown that SARS-CoV-2 transmissibility is limited to the first 3 days.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Human studies have found similar peak viral RNA levels for Alpha and Delta.
source: Human studies have found similar peak viral RNA levels for Alpha and Delta (Kissler et al., 2021; Elie et al., 2022) despite their epidemiological differences, including Delta's higher transmissibility (Earnest et al., 2022), shorter generation interval (Hart et al., 2022), and greater risk of severe disease (Twohig et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published human studies.

claim: Delta has higher transmissibility compared to Alpha.
source: Human studies have found similar peak viral RNA levels for Alpha and Delta (Kissler et al., 2021; Elie et al., 2022) despite their epidemiological differences, including Delta's higher transmissibility (Earnest et al., 2022), shorter generation interval (Hart et al., 2022), and greater risk of severe disease (Twohig et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Delta has a shorter generation interval compared to Alpha.
source: Human studies have found similar peak viral RNA levels for Alpha and Delta (Kissler et al., 2021; Elie et al., 2022) despite their epidemiological differences, including Delta's higher transmissibility (Earnest et al., 2022), shorter generation interval (Hart et al., 2022), and greater risk of severe disease (Twohig et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Delta has a greater risk of severe disease compared to Alpha.
source: Human studies have found similar peak viral RNA levels for Alpha and Delta (Kissler et al., 2021; Elie et al., 2022) despite their epidemiological differences, including Delta's higher transmissibility (Earnest et al., 2022), shorter generation interval (Hart et al., 2022), and greater risk of severe disease (Twohig et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There is a period early in infection (around 24 hr post-infection in inoculated hamsters) when oral swabs show high infectious virus titers, but air samples show low or undetectable levels of virus.
source: Crucially, there is a period early in infection (around 24 hr post-infection in inoculated hamsters) when oral swabs show high infectious virus titers, but air samples show low or undetectable levels of virus.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: Viral shedding should not be treated as a single quantity that rises and falls synchronously throughout the host.
source: Viral shedding should not be treated as a single quantity that rises and falls synchronously throughout the host; spatial models of infection may be required to identify the best correlates of airborne infectiousness (Snedden et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in breathing patterns were observed as early as 2 days post inoculation, preceding clinical symptoms, but coinciding with the window of time when infectious virus was detected in the air.
source: However, we did observed changes in breathing patterns as early as 2 DPI, preceding clinical symptoms, but coinciding with the window of time when infectious virus was detected in the air.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from whole body plethysmography and air sampling.

claim: The majority of SARS-CoV-2 exhaled from hamsters was observed within droplet nuclei <5 μm in size.
source: The majority of SARS-CoV-2 exhaled from hamsters was observed within droplet nuclei <5  μm in size (Kissler et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A rise in <0.53 μm particles and a drop in particles in the 1–10 μm range after infection was observed.
source: We report a rise in <0.53 μm particles and a drop in particles in the 1–10 μm range after infection.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from aerodynamic particle sizing.

claim: Humans with COVID-19 have been shown to exhale fewer particles than uninfected individuals during normal breathing, but not during coughing.
source: Humans with COVID-19 have been shown to exhale fewer particles than uninfected individuals during normal breathing, but not during coughing (Viklund et al., 2022) and fine aerosols have been found to be the major source of virus-loaded droplets.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Fine aerosols have been found to be the major source of virus-loaded droplets.
source: Humans with COVID-19 have been shown to exhale fewer particles than uninfected individuals during normal breathing, but not during coughing (Viklund et al., 2022) and fine aerosols have been found to be the major source of virus-loaded droplets.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from published literature.

claim: A shorter duration of measurable infectious virus in air, as opposed to the upper respiratory tract, could be partially due to early changes in airway constriction and a reduction in exhaled particles of the optimal size range for transmission.
source: This suggests that a shorter duration of measurable infectious virus in air, as opposed to the upper respiratory tract, could be partially due to early changes in airway constriction and a reduction in exhaled particles of the optimal size range for transmission.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation based on experimental observations.

claim: No clear transmission advantage for Delta over Alpha was found in Syrian hamsters in either an attack rate simulation or when comparing intra- and inter-host competitiveness over multiple generations of airborne transmission.
source: We did not find a clear transmission advantage for Delta over Alpha in Syrian hamsters, in either an attack rate simulation or when comparing intra- and inter-host competitiveness over multiple generations of airborne transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the attack rate and transmission chain experiments.

claim: The Syrian hamster model may not completely recapitulate all aspects of SARS-CoV-2 virus kinetics and transmission in humans.
source: The Syrian hamster model may not completely recapitulate all aspects of SARS-CoV-2 virus kinetics and transmission in humans, particularly as the virus continues to adapt to its human host.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about model limitations.

claim: At the time of emergence of Delta, a large part of the human population was either previously exposed to and/or vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.
source: Moreover, at the time of emergence of Delta, a large part of the human population was either previously exposed to and/or vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2; that underlying host immune landscape also affects the relative fitness of variants.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the epidemiological context.

claim: The naïve animal model does not capture the high prevalence of pre-existing immunity present in the human population.
source: Our naïve animal model does not capture the high prevalence of pre-existing immunity present in the human population and may therefore be less relevant for studying overall variant fitness in the current epidemiological context.
evidence: The claim is a statement about model limitations based on inference.

claim: Analyses of the cross-neutralization between Alpha and Delta suggest subtly different antigenic profiles.
source: Analyses of the cross-neutralization between Alpha and Delta suggest subtly different antigenic profiles (van Doremalen et al., 2022), and Delta's faster kinetics in humans may have also helped it cause more reinfections and 'breakthrough' infections (Yang and Shaman, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Delta's faster kinetics in humans may have helped it cause more reinfections and 'breakthrough' infections.
source: Analyses of the cross-neutralization between Alpha and Delta suggest subtly different antigenic profiles (van Doremalen et al., 2022), and Delta's faster kinetics in humans may have also helped it cause more reinfections and 'breakthrough' infections (Yang and Shaman, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: When sentinel hamsters were sequentially exposed, first to Alpha and then to Delta, generally no dual infections were observed.
source: When sentinel hamsters were sequentially exposed, first to Alpha and then to Delta, generally no dual infections—both variants detectable—were observed.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: When hamsters were exposed simultaneously to one donor infected with Alpha and another infected with Delta, mixed-variant virus populations in sentinels were detected in one of the cages (Cage F).
source: In contrast, when we exposed hamsters simultaneously to one donor infected with Alpha and another infected with Delta, we were able to detect mixed-variant virus populations in sentinels in one of the cages (Cage F, Appendix 1—figures 2–4).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the attack rate experiment.

claim: Virus population bottlenecks at the point of transmission depend on exposure mode and duration, as well as donor host shedding.
source: The fact that we saw both single-lineage and multi-lineage transmission events suggests that virus population bottlenecks at the point of transmission do indeed depend on exposure mode and duration, as well as donor host shedding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Mixed variant infections were not retained equally, and the relative variant frequencies differed between investigated compartments of the respiratory tract.
source: Mixed variant infections were not retained equally, and the relative variant frequencies differed between investigated compartments of the respiratory tract, suggesting roles for randomness or host-and-tissue specific differences in virus fitness.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from sequencing of different tissue compartments.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 circulates continuously in the human population, but many transmission chains are self-limiting, while rarer superspreading events account for a substantial fraction of the virus's total transmission.
source: Namely, SARS-CoV-2 circulates continuously in the human population, but many transmission chains are self-limiting, while rarer superspreading events account for a substantial fraction of the virus's total transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Some infected humans release tens to thousands of SARS-CoV-2 virions/min.
